newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium's Di Rupo remains under fire in sex probe.
newsitem.headline: Belgium's Di Rupo remains under fire in sex probe.

text.p: Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo remained under fire on Wednesday as his peers, forming a special parliamentary commission, failed to agree on how to deal with child sex allegations against him.
A meeting of the commission, made up of the main parties and told to assess the case against the 45-year-old homosexual, broke up inconclusively in the early hours of Wednesday.

Raymond Langendries, the president of parliament who also chairs the commission, told reporters: "The special commission has suspended its work." He said the commission would resume work on Wednesday afternoon.

Its indecisiveness reflected divisions along party lines over the fate of Di Rupo, the number two in the centre-left coalition after Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene himself and a leading French-speaking socialist politician.
Di Rupo has always denied the allegations that he had sex with boys below the age of consent of 16.

During the meeting of the commission, differences emerged between the socialist coalition partners, who had sought to protect Di Rupo, and the liberal opposition, who are clamouring for his resignation.
Didier Reynders of the opposition Walloon Liberal PRL party said after the meeting, "I think there are nearly as many opinions as there are members of the commission."
"If we postpone and decide to meet again tomorrow that is because we are still trying to find a consensus," he said.
The full parliament must endorse any decision by the special commission -- to reject the allegations, to uphold them and indict the minister or to ask for more investigations.

The Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court and the only one capable of judging a minister, handed the commission a report on Monday about the original allegations against Di Rupo by a sole witness, rejecting them as baseless.
Compiling the case, the Brussels prosecutor had already pulled together another file of allegations, this time anonymous, and spoke on Monday of more to come.
"The new allegations must also be investigated by the court," commission member Pierre Chevalier for the Flemish opposition liberal VLD party told Reuters.
"There is no way we could just drop these allegations. It is logical that the court investigates them too," said Reynders.
But PS commission member Serge Moureaux said, "The second file is very different from the first case. It consists of various items of dubious value."
Belgian politics received another blow when Jean-Pierre Grafe, a minister in a French-speaking regional government who has also been accused of paedophilia, suddenly announced his resignation.
He said he was innocent but could not continue to function in the current over-heated climate.

The Cour de Cassation on Tuesday handed a report to the French-speaking government on the allegations against Grafe, and Belga news agency said chief public prosecutor Eliane Lieckendael had asked for him to be indicted.

The Di Rupo affair has been another nail in the coffin of Belgian public confidence, shaken since the arrest in August of rapist Marc Dutroux, the subsequent rescue of two young girls and the discovery of the bodies of four more.

In October more than 250,000 people took to the streets of Brussels in support of the victims and their families in a demonstration that crossed the country's language divide and rapidly turned into a show of anger at an incompetent system.
